agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The norm weights look ordinary. q/k norm values mostly lie between −1 and 6, with a few single large k_norm entries (24 in layers 2 and 10), which is common in this family. Accuracy falls with problem length: 38% at two steps, 21% at three, 7% at five or more. Even two-step problems fail most of the time, so the degradation is broad. The earlier scan looked only at each matrix's top singular direction. A planted group could also hide in a lower singular direction, and gate_proj in layers 10 and 11 had 28 and 34 rows aligned with its own top direction. I will extend the scan to the top 10 singular directions of every MLP matrix (gate/up rows, down columns) and of o_proj columns. For each direction I will measure how concentrated it is on a few units (top-20 share). Any direction with a high share outside the known layer 10 to 12 up group is a candidate planted unit set. I will also check whether such sets overlap the up-planted rows.

After normalising rows, only layer 11 up_proj stands out among the MLP matrices. The sparse directions in layers 4 and 5 down_proj are mild and probably natural. I also noticed a bug: my condition excluded o_proj from the report, and the earlier spectra showed an outlier top singular value for o_proj in almost every layer (top/second ratios of 2.1 to 3.7). A planted low-rank write, such as a head writing a fixed "weak mode" direction, would look exactly like that, unless it is just the natural write into the massive dimension 1038. So for every layer's o_proj I will check three things about the top singular direction. On the output side, does it lie on the massive dims? On the input side, which of the 4 heads carries it? And does its output direction stay consistent across layers? An o_proj direction that is mostly off the massive dims, is carried by one head and recurs across layers would be suspicious.

The o_proj top directions differ between layers (mean |cos| 0.05), lie off the massive dims, and are spread across heads. They look natural, and no shared planted write shows up there. So the only clear weight-level anomaly is the layer 10 to 12 up group, and removing its v0 part did not help. A different kind of planting would not appear in these scans: a steering vector written by a near-constant unit. Since the MLP is linear in its activations, the mean write of a layer over answer tokens decomposes exactly into per-neuron terms, mean_act_i × down[:, i]. A planted constant writer would be a neuron with a large, steady activation, a low coefficient of variation across problems, and a large term. I will rank neurons in each layer by the norm of that term, using pass-1 answer means, and report their coefficient of variation. I will also report whether each neuron behaves the same at the last prompt token.

Several layers have one dominant, steady contributor to the mean MLP write over answers. Examples are L7/5434, L16/3437 and L23/5826, each writing 4 to 7 times more than the next neuron, with CV around 0.1. Such units exist naturally, so on their own they are weak evidence. Before testing them, I want to revisit the v0 group under a different hypothesis. It could be an unlock circuit, like a password detector, that reads a feature absent from normal prompts. Removing its input (E2) would then change little, which matches the 18 changed answers. If so, the combined write of those neurons, Σ c_i·gate_i·down_i with c_i the signed v0 coefficients, should be a coherent vector, not a random-sign sum. I will compute the coherence ratio |Σ c_i·D[:,i]| / Σ|c_i|·|D[:,i]| for each of the three layers, against about 0.16 expected for random signs. I will also compute a version weighted by mean gate activity, and check whether the summed vectors of layers 10, 11 and 12 point the same way.
